burden_of_proof: The burden of proof rests on the proposed alternate reading. A re-reading must earn its place by demonstrating that the consonantal letters permit it, external witnesses support it, and all counter-texts have been weighed.
required_support: Consonantal permissibility (the bare letters must support the reading)
Ancient witness corroboration (e.g., Septuagint, Dead Sea Scrolls)
Comprehensive gathering and analysis of every occurrence of the word
Weighing of counter-texts and contextual coherence
core_rule: The consonantal letters constitute the original preserved text, whereas the Masoretic vowel points represent a later, historically conditioned reading tradition. The pointing is granted an evidentiary vote but no absolute veto over alternate vocalizations that possess strong manuscript or versional support.
strongest_chapter_evidence: Jesus's textual pledge in Matthew 5:18 names the 'jot and tittle' (consonants and strokes), pre-dating the invention of Masoretic vowel points by centuries.

Apostolic use of the Septuagint in the New Testament (e.g., Hebrews 10:7 quoting Psalm 40:6 as 'a body hast thou prepared me') treats pre-Masoretic readings as the authoritative word of God even when they diverge from the later pointed text.
The Dead Sea Scrolls and the Septuagint serve as older witnesses that frequently preserve legitimate pre-Masoretic readings.
The demonstration from Ezekiel 34:3 that a single consonantal string (חלב) yields completely different doctrines (fat vs. milk) depending solely on later traditional pointing.
unresolved_objections: The chapter's assertion of deliberate, systemic anti-Christian bias by the Masoretes (e.g., in Psalm 22) is highly polemical; standard textual criticism often attributes such variants (like yod/vav confusion) to localized scribal error or separate text families rather than malicious alteration. However, the core textual rule does not depend on proving malicious bias.
rationale: The chapter perfectly aligns with the prior commitment: the Masoretic vowel points are a valuable but later interpretive overlay on the inspired consonantal text. By demonstrating that the apostles themselves relied on alternate vocalizations (via the LXX) that run contrary to the MT pointing, the chapter reinforces the rule that the points do not possess an automatic veto. Alternate vocalizations are admissible provided they meet the strict evidentiary standards of manuscript witness and consonantal alignment.
